summary.text: The giant squid is a deep-ocean squid found in all the world's oceans, with females reaching about 5 m from the rear fins to the arm tips.
Its eyes, up to at least 27 cm across, are the largest of any living creature except perhaps the colossal squid, and help it catch scarce light in deep water.
Instead of a gas-filled swim bladder, it stays buoyant with an ammonium chloride solution lighter than seawater, which also makes it unappealing as food.

items.prompt: A sperm whale is found with circular scars on and around its head. What most likely made them?

options.label: Bites from a pack of sharks
Suckers of a giant squid it attacked
Scraping against rocky seafloor
Barnacles that fell off its skin

items.explain: Sperm whales that attack giant squid commonly carry round scars from the squid's suckers near their heads.

items.prompt: Most fish stay afloat using a gas-filled swim bladder. How does a giant squid keep from sinking?

options.label: A gas-filled sac much like a fish
Constant swimming with its fins
A body fluid lighter than seawater
Oil stored in a very large liver

items.explain: An ammonium chloride solution throughout its body is lighter than seawater, giving it neutral buoyancy.

items.prompt: How do its enormous eyes help a giant squid in the deep ocean?

options.label: They let it tell colours apart
They gather more of the scarce light
They scare away its predators
They help it sense water pressure

items.explain: Large eyes detect light better, and light is scarce in deep water; the squid probably cannot see colour.

items.prompt: How can scientists estimate how old a giant squid was?

options.label: By measuring the length of its arms
By counting suckers on its tentacles
By weighing its parrot-like beak
By counting rings in its balance organ

items.explain: The statolith inside the statocyst, the organ that senses orientation, has growth rings that can be counted like a tree's.

items.prompt: The giant squid is longer than the colossal squid. How do the two compare in weight?

options.label: The giant squid is much lighter
The giant squid is much heavier
They weigh almost exactly the same
The giant squid is twice as heavy

items.explain: The giant squid is less robust and much of its length is arms, so it is substantially lighter.

items.prompt: When a giant squid needs to move quickly, what does it do?

options.label: Beats its rear fins very rapidly
Pulls itself along with its arms
Jets water out through its siphon
Releases gas bubbles to push off

items.explain: It fills its mantle cavity with water, then contracts muscles to jet the water out through the siphon.

paragraphs.heading: A giant of the deep
paragraphs.text: The giant squid, Architeuthis dux, is a squid of the deep ocean and one of the largest invertebrates alive. Females can reach about 5 m from the rear fins to the tips of the long arms, and males are a little shorter. That makes it longer than the colossal squid, estimated at 4.2 m, but much lighter, and the colossal squid is the only mollusc that outranks it. Scientists once argued over how many giant squid species exist, but genetic work points to just one. In 2004 a Japanese team took the first pictures of a live one in its natural home.

paragraphs.heading: Long arms, light body
paragraphs.text: Like every squid, it has a mantle, which is its main body, plus eight arms and two longer tentacles. The mantle is about 2 m long, while the two feeding tentacles, hidden away in life, stretch to 10 m. These are the longest tentacles known among cephalopods, the animal group squid belong to. Because arms and tentacles make up so much of its length, it is far lighter than its main predator, the sperm whale, and well-documented specimens weigh hundreds of kilograms rather than thousands. Reports of animals 20 m or longer have never been backed by scientific records.

paragraphs.heading: Suckers and a beak
paragraphs.text: The inner sides of the arms and tentacles carry hundreds of rounded suckers, each 2 to 5 cm across and set on a stalk. Around each sucker's rim runs a sharp ring with fine teeth. The pull of the cups and the bite of these teeth together fasten the squid to its prey. Sperm whales that have attacked giant squid often carry round sucker scars on or near the head. All the arms and tentacles rise from a circle around a single beak shaped like a parrot's.

paragraphs.heading: Jetting and floating
paragraphs.text: Small fins at the back of the mantle help it move, and like other cephalopods it travels by jet propulsion: it draws water into its mantle and pushes it out through its siphon in gentle, steady pulses. For a burst of speed it fills the cavity wide and then squeezes hard. It breathes with two large gills inside the mantle and, like other squid, carries dark ink. Instead of the gas-filled swim bladder most fish use, it stays afloat with an ammonium chloride solution spread through its body that is lighter than seawater. That solution tastes a bit like salty liquorice, which makes the animal unappealing as everyday food for people.

paragraphs.heading: Eyes for the dark
paragraphs.text: The giant squid has some of the largest eyes of any living animal, at least 27 cm across with a 9 cm pupil; only the colossal squid may rival it. Big eyes gather more light, including the light of glowing animals, and light is scarce in deep water. The squid probably cannot see color, but it can likely tell apart small differences in shade, which matters in the dim deep ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Where it lives and how old
paragraphs.text: Giant squid live in every ocean, usually near the slopes of continents and islands, from Newfoundland and Norway to southern Africa, Japan and New Zealand. They are rare in tropical and polar waters. How deep they go is not fully known, but trawl catches and the dives of sperm whales suggest a range of possibly 300 to 1,000 m. Their age can be read from growth rings in the statolith, part of the statocyst organs they use to sense their position and motion, much like counting a tree's rings. Much of what is known about their age comes from those rings and from beaks left undigested in sperm whale stomachs.
